summary: Phú Thọ — the Đất Tổ, the ancestral land of the nation — has a plain, homely cuisine stamped by the Mường people and the midland farmers, above all thịt chua Thanh Sơn, pork fermented inside a bamboo tube, and bánh tai, a plain-rice cake with a pork filling. Alongside these, the produce of the cọ palm, such as cọ ỏm, is a culinary trait of the northern midlands that is hard to find anywhere else.

thit-chua-thanh-son.description: Thịt chua Thanh Sơn is a plain dish of the Mường people of Thanh Sơn district, Phú Thọ, born of the old need to keep meat for a long time in the uplands. Pork belly and shoulder are sliced thin, seasoned, then tossed with finely ground thính (roasted ground rice), packed tight into a bamboo tube or a box and left to ferment naturally for three to five days. The result has a gentle sourness and a springy, crunchy skin against the nutty fragrance of the thính, making it the best-known speciality of the Đất Tổ.
keyIngredients: Pork belly and shoulder (with the skin on)
A bamboo tube or box for the fermenting
prepOutline: Wash the pork, drain it and slice it thin into bite-sized pieces
Season with salt and black pepper and let it take up the flavour
Toss the meat with thính (roasted ground rice) until every piece is coated
Pack it tightly into a bamboo tube or box and leave it somewhere cool and airy for three to five days to sour
thit-chua-thanh-son.howToEat: Roll thịt chua up in lá sung (young fig leaf), young guava leaf or other astringent leaves and dip it in chilli sauce; it is usually eaten with grilled bánh đa (rice cracker) and goes especially well cold with beer in summer.

banh-tai-phu-tho.description: Bánh tai, also called bánh hòn, is the well-known homely breakfast of Phú Thọ town, made from plain rice soaked and pounded to a smooth dough around a filling of slightly fatty pork, dried shallot and pepper. The maker shapes the dough into a curve like an ear, closes it over the filling and steams it. The cake is simple but demands a deft, patient hand at every stage so the wrapper turns out springy and does not fall apart in the steamer.
prepOutline: Rinse the plain rice, soak it for three to four hours, then pound or mill it into a dough
Roll the dough into balls, parboil for about 20 minutes, then pound it smooth again
Make the filling from finely pounded pork mixed with dried shallot, pepper and salt
Shape the dough around the filling into an ear-like curve and steam for about 30 minutes
banh-tai-phu-tho.howToEat: Bánh tai is eaten hot straight from the steamer, usually for breakfast, and can be dipped in nước mắm (Vietnamese fish sauce) with chilli to taste.

co-om-phu-tho.description: Cọ ỏm is a plain, characteristic dish of the Phú Thọ midlands, made from the fruit of the cọ palm — the tree bound up with the landscape of the Đất Tổ. The fruit is peeled and then "ỏm" (steeped) in water of about 80 degrees C, held at a bare simmer until the palm oil rises to the surface and the fruit turns from dark green to a glossy yellow. Cọ ỏm has a distinctive rich, nutty taste with a faint astringency rather than sweetness or strong perfume — a very particular kind of plainness in the cooking of the Đất Tổ.
prepOutline: Choose sticky-fleshed cọ fruit at just-ripe stage, scrape off the outer bloom and wash clean
Heat water with a little salt until it barely trembles (about 80 degrees C)
Drop in the fruit, keep the heat low and stir gently so everything stays submerged
Om (steep gently) until the palm oil rises to the surface and the fruit turns yellow, then take it off the heat
co-om-phu-tho.howToEat: Cọ ỏm is eaten as it is while still warm, peeling out the rich, nutty flesh; it is usually given as a gift from the countryside or eaten with rice as a homely dish of the Phú Thọ locals.
